patterns_data.pattern_details: CT PPO acute hospital spend rose sharply in admissions that required authorization, and the increase came from both more use and higher paid amounts per admission. The biggest pressure sits in very high-acuity inpatient cases, especially craniotomy and sepsis, with some additional volume concentration at Manchester Memorial Hospital. This is not a broad product trend; it is a concentrated inpatient cost event in CT.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: This is the single largest identified driver and needs immediate action because both utilization and severity-priced inpatient spend moved up together.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Run a CT PPO inpatient action plan that pairs UM review of PA-approved acute admissions with reimbursement review of high-cost neuro and sepsis cases, starting with admission criteria, level of care, and contract terms at the main contributing hospitals.
evidence_summary: CT PPO acute hospital admissions requiring authorization added about $18.8M from 284 more admissions and about $5.4K higher paid per admit.
Craniotomy cases added about $1.3M on 14 more admissions, with paid per admit up about $92.7K.
Sepsis without prolonged ventilation added about $350K on 16 more admissions.
Manchester Memorial Hospital added about $134K from 8 more admissions, indicating a local volume pocket within the larger CT pattern.

patterns_data.pattern_details: A small number of rare, very expensive neuro, spine, and complex post-surgical cases are driving a large share of spend growth. In CA, the pattern extends beyond acute hospital stays into long-term care hospital and physical rehab settings, which suggests downstream site-of-care and recovery-pathway costs as well. These are not broad population trends; they are concentrated outlier episodes that need case-based action.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Outlier episodes of this size can distort trend, create avoidable post-acute leakage, and require different actions than routine utilization management.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Open a focused case review on the largest neuro, spine, and complex surgical admissions and their post-acute transitions to confirm severity, medical necessity, and single-case or outlier payment terms before broader policy changes.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Most of the dollars come from low-volume, low-baseline cases, so chart and coding confirmation is needed before applying broad utilization or network actions.
evidence_summary: CA rare high-cost clinical cases added about $5.6M, led by traumatic subdural hematoma at about $1.0M, cerebral aneurysm at about $0.7M, benign cranial nerve neoplasm at about $0.7M, and orthopedic aftercare after amputation at about $0.5M.
A second rare-case cluster added about $2.7M, including complex spinal fusion at about $1.3M and a digestive O.R. case at about $0.7M.
CA EPO acute craniotomy alone added about $2.1M on 8 more admissions, with paid per admit up about $92.3K.
CA post-acute spillover added about $0.6M in long-term care hospital and about $0.3M in physical rehab, showing the pathway continues after the acute stay.

patterns_data.pattern_details: KY has two distinct acute hospital pressures at once: HMO spend is rising mainly from more admissions, while PPO spend is being pushed by higher paid amounts per admission even as admissions fall. That means a single response will miss the root causes. UM actions are more relevant on the HMO side, while rate or reimbursement review matters more on the PPO side.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: KY is large enough to matter financially, but the operating levers differ by product and authorization status.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Split the KY response by product: review HMO PA-approved acute admissions for avoidable growth, and separately review PPO acute hospital reimbursement for non-PA cases with rising paid per admit.

patterns_data.pattern_details: A meaningful amount of spend is sitting in claims with facility type marked as Not Mapped, especially in CT and KY. That prevents reliable site-of-care, provider, and authorization interpretation and can send operational teams after the wrong lever. This should be treated as a gating data-quality issue before any broad network or UM response.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: When facility type is missing, site-of-care strategy, contract action, and authorization policy can all be misdirected.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Repair facility mapping for the Not Mapped claims in CT, KY, and VA, restate the spend by true facility type and provider, and only then decide whether the issue is acute hospital, rehab, LTCH, or another setting.
patterns_data.validation_reason: Facility type is explicitly unmapped, so site-of-care attribution is unreliable until the claims are reclassified.
evidence_summary: CT Not Mapped facility claims added about $4.3M on 48 more admissions, with paid per admit up about $31.2K.
KY Not Mapped facility claims added about $773K on 12 more admissions.
VA Not Mapped claims are smaller at about $48K, but show the same classification risk.

patterns_data.pattern_details: Several states show material spend movement tied to authorization code distribution rather than a confirmed change in utilization or reimbursement. Until the authorization coding logic is reconciled, the apparent change could reflect classification movement instead of true operational performance. This is a gating validation pattern, not a ready-for-action cost trend.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Misreading code movement as medical or provider performance can trigger the wrong UM or contracting decisions.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Reconcile authorization-required coding and mapping between source systems and claims in CA, TX, GA, and WI, then restate the affected trends before taking provider or policy action.
patterns_data.validation_reason: The groups are explicitly flagged as authorization or mapping shifts that require validation before action.
evidence_summary: CA authorization code movement accounted for about $1.9M, mostly in craniotomy at about $1.7M and musculoskeletal aftercare at about $0.3M.
TX authorization code movement was mixed but net positive at about $0.6M, with a neuro increase offset partly by a sepsis decrease.
GA and WI added about $0.5M of additional authorization code movement, led by chemotherapy-related claims.

patterns_data.pattern_details: Inpatient chemotherapy is emerging as a distinct spend pattern, led by WI and supported by smaller acute-facility signals in OH and CA. The growth reflects both more admissions and higher paid amounts per admission, which makes this different from a simple coding fluctuation. Because oncology actions differ from general inpatient management, this should stay separate from other clinical patterns.
patterns_data.why_it_matters: Oncology admissions often have different authorization, site-of-care, and care-management options than general medical admissions.
patterns_data.recommended_next_step: Review inpatient chemotherapy authorization criteria and alternate-site-of-care opportunities, starting with WI, to determine whether some treatment can safely shift out of inpatient acute settings.
evidence_summary: WI inpatient chemotherapy added about $0.9M on 26 more admissions, with paid per admit up about $25.7K.
WI POS acute chemotherapy added about $180K on 6 more admissions.
OH children's chemotherapy added about $142K on 4 more admissions.
CA EPO acute chemotherapy added about $140K with flat admissions, driven by about $70.1K higher paid per admit.
